rows.answer: He gives four related arguments, previewed at [spya-cv97j7]. The two doing most work are that brains can't be cleanly split into software and hardware [spya-zw2m7u], and that simulating something doesn't create it [spya-npjt4j]. He hedges: he says computational functionalism "may" be wrong [spya-wepmnr]. For your essay, read the four numbered sections from [spya-a8jgf4].

steps.words: What does he mean by the 'mythology' of conscious AI?
Which sections should I read closely as a philosophy student?

rows.answer: He never defines it in one line. The "mythology" is a set of unexamined assumptions and stories. The central one is that consciousness is just computation, an assumption "so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all" [spya-wepmnr]. The other is the techno-rapture dream [spya-v4sduf]. For the rest, read his claim that nothing here is inevitable [spya-hbueqc].

steps.words: Is his argument against the brain-as-computer idea actually convincing?
computational functionalism

rows.answer:
He offers three supports: no clean software/hardware split in brains [spya-zw2m7u], neurons that can't be swapped for silicon [spya-un9fjn], and time that matters physically [spya-v52g4f]. My guess is that the strongest part is aimed at Turing-style computation only, since he admits broader functionalism survives [spya-f0qxnb].

For your essay, check the concession at [spya-qu7j89].
